terms.gloss: put words together from their syllables
evidence: Quint. 1.1.31: tunc ipsīs syllabīs verba complectī et hīs sermōnem cōnectere incipiat
terms.comment: Quintilian’s description of the step after the letters: the child first joins letters surely, then takes in words by their syllables, and only then reads on at speed. Latin teaching went by syllables, not by single sounds.

evidence: Cic. Att. 13.25.3: syllabātim, of dictating (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Our combination: syllabātim is Cicero’s word for dictating one syllable at a time; with legere it is what a parent says to a child who is sounding a word out.

phrases.english: Don’t rush; sound it out: ca-pel-la.

phrases.latin: Syllabīs nūllum compendium est: perdiscendae omnēs
phrases.english: There is no shortcut with syllables: they must all be learnt thoroughly

phrases.latin: tunc ipsīs syllabīs verba complectī et hīs sermōnem cōnectere incipiat
phrases.english: then let him begin to take in words by their syllables and to join them into speech

sources: Lewis & Short: syllaba · Lewis & Short: complector · Lewis & Short: syllabatim
